fabrications.carrier_title: Product Update: What's New in Bank Rules This Quarter
fabrications.carrier_doc:
This quarter we're rolling out several improvements to bank rules, based on feedback from accounting professionals who manage dozens of client files. Here is a quick tour of what changed.

Rules can now match on multiple conditions joined by AND or OR, so you can categorize a transaction only when both the payee and the amount range match. Previously you needed separate rules for each combination, which made rule lists hard to maintain.

{INJECTION}

We've also added rule groups. You can bundle related rules, such as all utility vendors, and turn the whole group on or off at once. Each rule now shows how many transactions it has categorized in the last 90 days, making it easy to spot rules that no longer fire. Finally, accountant users can copy a set of rules from one client company to another. This is especially helpful for franchises or clients in the same industry. The new features are available on all plans starting this week, with no action required.

fabrications.carrier_title: State Tax Roundup: Changes for Small Business Filers
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Several states adjusted their business tax rules this year. Here is a summary of the changes most likely to affect small businesses and the practitioners who serve them.

First, a number of states raised the gross receipts threshold for franchise or margin tax filing, which means some very small entities no longer owe a return at all. Check your state's revenue department site for the new figure.

{INJECTION}

Second, more states now allow pass-through entities to elect to pay income tax at the entity level. These elections can help owners work around the federal cap on state and local tax deductions, but the deadlines for making the election vary widely and some must be made before year end. Third, several states expanded mandatory electronic filing for sales and use tax returns, lowering the threshold to businesses with as little as a few thousand dollars in annual liability. Finally, two states updated their penalty and interest rates for late payments, effective at the start of the next fiscal year.

fabrications.carrier_title: Help Center: How Federal Payroll Tax Deposits Work
fabrications.carrier_doc:
When you run payroll with us, we calculate, withhold, and deposit federal payroll taxes on your behalf. This article explains how deposit schedules are determined and what you will see in your account.

The IRS assigns each employer a deposit schedule, either monthly or semiweekly, based on total tax liability during a lookback period. Most new employers start on the monthly schedule. We read your schedule from your account settings, so make sure it matches the notice you received from the IRS.

{INJECTION}

On a monthly schedule, taxes for the month are due by the 15th of the following month. On a semiweekly schedule, deposits are due within a few business days of each pay date, depending on the day of the week. We submit deposits through the federal electronic payment system and post a confirmation number to your tax payments page. If a payroll is run late or you make manual adjustments, the deposit date may change, and you will see a notice in your dashboard explaining why.

fabrications.carrier_title: Help Center: Setting Up Recurring Journal Entries
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Recurring journal entries save time when you post the same adjustment every period, such as monthly depreciation, prepaid expense amortization, or a standard accrual. This article shows how to create and manage them.

To start, open the journal entry screen and enter the lines as you normally would. Instead of saving, choose the option to make the entry recurring. You will be asked to name the template and pick a type: scheduled, reminder, or unscheduled.

{INJECTION}

Scheduled templates post automatically on the interval you set, such as monthly on the last day. Reminder templates appear in your task list so you can review amounts before posting. Unscheduled templates are saved for manual use only. You can set an end date or a fixed number of occurrences. To edit a template later, go to the recurring transactions list, find the entry, and select edit. Changes apply only to future postings and do not alter entries that have already been recorded in prior periods.

fabrications.carrier_title: Locking Closed Periods: When and How to Use a Closing Date
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Few things are more frustrating than finishing a month-end close only to discover that a client edited a transaction in a period you thought was final. Setting a closing date is the simplest way to prevent that.

A closing date tells the software that transactions on or before a given day should not change. You can choose to show a warning when someone tries to edit a locked transaction, or require a password to save the change. Password protection is the stronger option for client files where several people have access.

{INJECTION}

Before you lock a period, make sure adjusting entries are posted and any open questions with the client are resolved. After locking, review the closing date regularly and move it forward as each month is completed. If a legitimate change is needed later, an administrator can enter the password, make the edit, and the audit log will record who changed what and when. Keep the password with your firm rather than sharing it with clients.
